flashcards.q: Give the 8-phase time budget for a 45-minute system design round.
flashcards.a: 2 restate + scope contract; 5 requirements (FR + NFR table); 5 numbers; 5 API contract; 7 data model; 8 architecture; 6 scale; 5 failure; 2 wrap. Hard constraint: architecture on the board by minute 32.

flashcards.q: What is the NFR checklist mnemonic and what does each letter stand for?
flashcards.a: SCALD-CoM: Scale, Consistency, Availability, Latency, Durability, Cost, Multi-tenancy/compliance. Ask 5-6 of the 7, not all of them, and write the answers in a table you refer back to by name.

flashcards.q: What makes a clarifying question high-value versus low-value?
flashcards.a: A high-value question names two concrete alternatives and states that they lead to different designs (read:write 100:1 vs 2:1; chronological vs ranked; fanout distribution with or without 50M-follower accounts). Low-value questions have answers you cannot act on (how many users, should it be scalable).

flashcards.q: Why write the API contract before drawing the architecture?
flashcards.a: The API is falsifiable and commits you to payload size, read/write split, pagination model, and the sync/async boundary. Once POST /follows returns 202, the async queue in the diagram is justified by the contract instead of being an unexplained box.

flashcards.q: Name the five cheap points to bank in an API-contract phase.
flashcards.a: Versioned path (/v1/); Idempotency-Key header on writes with stored key-to-response and a TTL beyond the retry window; cursor pagination not offset (offset skips and duplicates on insert-heavy lists); 202 to encode async work; explicit error codes including 429.

flashcards.q: What is the one line that matters most in the data-model phase?
flashcards.a: The partition key, plus a statement for each table of which query it serves and whether that query is single-partition. A relationship table like follows needs indexing in BOTH directions (follower_id for reads, followee_id for fanout).

flashcards.q: What is the derivation chain that makes the architecture phase mechanical?
flashcards.a: requirements decide which numbers matter; numbers decide whether one machine suffices; API decides read/write split and payload size; data model decides the partition key; partition key decides which queries are cheap; architecture is then DERIVED and every box traces to a line above it.

flashcards.q: In the scale phase, what must you produce per component?
flashcards.a: The specific limit it hits first, the number, and the fix. Then RANK the bottlenecks (which breaks first at 10x and why it beats the runners-up), and attach a cost figure with the dominant line item named.

flashcards.q: What three things must a failure-mode statement include?
flashcards.a: What the user sees, what the operator sees (the observable symptom in a log, metric, or trace), and the recovery. Volunteering one named non-obvious failure mode with its symptom is the highest-value unprompted sentence in the round.

flashcards.q: What are the three wrap-up sentences at minute 43?
flashcards.a: What you would build first (smallest thing that serves the first million users), the biggest risk you are accepting (usually a guessed tuning parameter you would instrument), and what you would cut under cost pressure.

flashcards.q: How do you handle a blocked clarifying question the interviewer refuses to answer?
flashcards.a: State the assumption, state its consequence, and move: assume 100:1 read:write; if it is closer to 2:1 the precomputed timeline stops paying for itself and I flip to read-time merge. Converting a blocked question into a demonstrated tradeoff scores better than the answer would have.

flashcards.q: You discover at minute 30 that an assumption was wrong. What is the recovery protocol?
flashcards.a: Say it precisely (name the statistical error, not just the number), do NOT restart, identify the one or two decisions it feeds, walk the branch you already named, and state what you would measure to fix the assumption for real. Keep the old number visible and annotated.

flashcards.q: What changed about system design interviews in 2026?
flashcards.a: The passing bar rose; AI/LLM infrastructure prompts moved into general engineering loops (roughly half of loops now include an ML-adjacent question, up from ~1 in 10 in 2024); and interviewers now grade cost, so a design with no dollar figure reads as junior.

flashcards.q: Three extra NFR rows for an LLM-in-the-loop prompt.
flashcards.a: Token/cost budget (enforced in code as a per-user per-day cap, not a hope); non-determinism, meaning an eval/regression suite plus an online quality metric; and blast radius, meaning prompt-injection surface and the scope of actions an agent may take. Plus a deterministic fallback for when budget or model fails.

flashcards.q: How does the method change per company style?
flashcards.a: Meta: 45 min, breadth then interviewer-steered depth, so protect 15 minutes for the deep dive. Google: naming a component invites you to implement it, so name fewer. Amazon: expand failure and rollout phases. Stripe: API and data model scored hardest, so expand phase 3. AI-infra: add token/eval/blast-radius NFRs.

flashcards.q: Two candidates draw the same final diagram; one passes. What separates them?
flashcards.a: Traceability of derivation, which shows up under mutation. Change the read:write ratio or the follower distribution and the candidate who derived adjusts one decision, while the one who recalled has nothing to adjust and must defend or restart. Interviewers mutate prompts specifically to find this out.
